source_text:
Praeclara quaedam res est silentium, tum aliis plerumque permultis, tum mihi nunc vel maxime, qui volens nolensque clausum os habeo, et tacere cogor. Inexercitatus enim sum ac plane rudis sermonum illorum elegantium atque ornatorum, qui selectis, probatisque nominibus ac verbis, perpetuo quodam et inoffenso ductu pronuntiantur aut componuntur: fortasse a natura ipsa ad venustum hoc, et vere Graecanicum opus elaborandum minus comparatus. Sed et octavus iam annus est, ex quo nec brevem, longamve orationem ullam habui ipse, nec aut scripsi; nec alium audivi quem vel privatim scribentem, historiamve, vel publice panegyricos sermones, controversiasque declamantem, praeter hosce admirabiles viros, qui pulchram philosophiam amplexi sunt: quibus scilicet elocutionis, elegantiaeque verborum cura minor est; postpositis autem vocibus, res ipsas, ut se habeant, accurate singulas investigare et enuntiare volunt: non quod alterum illud nolint, opinor; quin volunt quam maxime praeclaras, et accuratas cogitationes suas praeclaro et omnis mendacii experte sermone exprimere: sed quod fortasse non possint, nec adeo sic in promptu; hinc sacram ac divinam facultatem propriis explicare sententiis; hinc orationem verbis comptam atque concinnam adferre; et quae duorum hominum propria cuiusque est praerogativa, una et eadem, eaque parva et humana mente complecti; praesertim cum utriusque dispar ac penitus contraria sit ratio. Cogitationi siquidem, inventionique rerum amicum quodammodo, et consors operis est silentium: dicendi vero facultatem, et pronunciationis dignitatem haud alibi reperias, quam in verbis, verborumque assidua meditatione ac usu. Quin etiam et alia quaedam mentem disciplina vehementer occupat, et os linguam plane constringit, si vel exiguum quippiam Graeca voce eloqui velim: mirificae nimirum leges nostrae, quibus omnium nunc, qui Romanorum imperio parent, res gubernantur: quae quidem neque conduntur, neque percipiuntur sine labore ac molestia; et sapientes quidem illae, piaeque sunt et variae, et suspiciendae, atque ut uno verbo dicam, Graecissimae: ceterum Romano expositae, traditaeque sermone, admirabili sane atque magnifico, et ad imperii maiestatem confirmato; sed mihi gravi nihilominus ac difficili. Non enim aliter sentire aut posse aut velle me unquam dixerim. Cum autem aliud nihil sint voces nostrae, quam imagines quaedam animi nostri conceptuum ac notionum; iis quidem, qui dicendi facultate valent, tanquam pictoribus quibusdam et arte peritissimis, et colorum copia instructissimis, non similes modo, sed varias etiam, et ad speciem crebra florum admixtione pulcherrimas pingere licere sine ullo impedimento, confitendum est.

Nos vero, quasi pauperes quidam, variis huiusmodi fucis carentes, et qui vel nunquam eos in arte nostra habuerimus, vel eos fortasse abiecerimus; tanquam solis carbonibus aut testulis viratorum, communiumque nominum ac verborum, prima animi nostri sensa, iis quae supersunt vocibus depingentes effingimus; typorum animi characteres, si non claros, nec ad speciem ornatos; at quemadmodum in carbonum pictura fieri solet, quoquo modo representare conantes; si quid uspiam venustum ac disertum se offerat, sponte nostra, ut qui haec aspernemur, reicientes. Verum et tertium quiddam rursum aliud est, quod impedit, et avocat, et multo magis, quam cetera, nos retinet, silentioque uti iubet, argumentum nempe ipsum; de quo dicere auebam quidem, sed cunctari nunc cogor, et haereo. De viro enim dicere institui, qui homo quidem esse videtur, et talis apparet; iis vero, qui magnitudinem eius habitus, moresque intueri possunt, maioribus quibusdam ornamentis instructus ac prope divinis videatur.
thought_title: Silence, poverty of speech, and the daunting subject
orientation: Gregory is opening his address to Origen by explaining why he has been silent for eight years and why he now hesitates to speak.
pass_a_gloss: A certain excellent thing is silence, both for very many others generally, and for me now especially, who willingly and unwillingly have a closed mouth, and am compelled to be silent. For I am untrained and plainly ignorant of those elegant and adorned speeches, which with select and approved names and words are pronounced or composed in a continuous and unbroken course: perhaps by nature itself less fitted for elaborating this charming and truly Greek work. But it is now the eighth year, since I neither had any short or long speech myself, nor wrote; nor heard another either privately writing, or a history, or publicly declaiming panegyric speeches and controversies, except these admirable men, who have embraced beautiful philosophy: for whom, of course, the care of elocution and elegance of words is less; but having set aside words, they wish to investigate accurately and declare the things themselves, each one, as they are: not that they do not wish the other thing, I think; indeed they wish as much as possible to express their excellent and accurate thoughts in excellent speech free from all falsehood: but because perhaps they cannot, nor is it so readily at hand; on the one hand to explain the sacred and divine faculty in their own sentences; on the other hand to bring forward speech adorned and polished with words; and to embrace in one and the same, and that small and human, mind the prerogative proper to each of two men; especially since the method of each is different and utterly contrary. For to thought and the discovery of things, silence is in a way friendly and a partner of the work: but the faculty of speaking and the dignity of delivery you would find nowhere else than in words, and in assiduous meditation and use of words. Moreover also another discipline violently occupies the mind, and plainly constrains the mouth and tongue, if I wish to say even a tiny thing in the Greek voice: our wonderful laws, of course, by which the affairs of all who now obey the Roman empire are governed: which indeed are neither established nor learned without labor and trouble; and they are wise, and pious, and varied, and to be admired, and to say in one word, most Greek: but set forth and handed down in the Roman language, admirable indeed and magnificent, and confirmed to the majesty of the empire; but nevertheless heavy and difficult for me. For I would never say that I could or wished to feel otherwise. But since our words are nothing other than certain images of the concepts and notions of our mind; it must be confessed that for those who are strong in the faculty of speaking, as for certain painters both most skilled in art and most furnished with an abundance of colors, it is permitted to paint not only similar but also varied images, and most beautiful by frequent admixture of flowers to the appearance, without any hindrance. But we, as certain poor men, lacking various dyes of this kind, and who either never had them in our art, or perhaps threw them away; as if with charcoal alone or potsherds of common and ordinary names and words, painting the first perceptions of our mind with the words that remain, we fashion them; the characters of the impressions of the mind, if not clear, nor adorned to appearance; but as is accustomed to happen in charcoal painting, trying to represent them in whatever way; if anything charming and eloquent offers itself anywhere, of our own accord, as those who despise these things, rejecting it. But there is again a certain third other thing, which hinders, and calls away, and much more than the rest holds us back, and bids us use silence, namely the subject itself; about which I was eager indeed to speak, but I am now compelled to hesitate, and I stick. For I have resolved to speak about a man, who indeed seems to be a man, and appears such; but to those who can look upon the greatness of his character and his habits, he would seem furnished with certain greater and almost divine ornaments.

choices.why: The glossary mandates 'silence' for silentium, and it fits the opening claim that silence is an excellent thing.
Keeps the plural and the demonstrative force, matching Gregory's contrast between polished rhetoric and his own plainness.
Preserves the adjective's cultural force; Gregory is contrasting Greek rhetorical craft with the Roman tongue of the laws.
Uses the glossary English for both terms, keeping the humble, material metaphor of painting with poor means.

choices.english: the characters of the impressions of the mind
choices.why: Keeps the technical metaphor of impressions and their characters, matching the glossary sense for typorum.
rejected: the marks of the mind's images

choices.why: The glossary mandates 'divine' for divinis, and it captures the near-divine ornaments attributed to Origen.

pass_b_english: Silence is an excellent thing—for many others, most of the time, but for me now especially, since I keep my mouth shut whether I want to or not, and I am forced to be silent. I am untrained and completely unskilled in those elegant and adorned speeches that are delivered or composed with carefully chosen and approved names and words, in one continuous and unbroken flow. Perhaps I was simply not equipped by nature to produce this charming and truly Greek work. But it is now the eighth year since I myself have delivered any speech, short or long, or written anything, or heard anyone else—whether writing privately or composing history, or publicly declaiming panegyrics and debates—except for these admirable men who have embraced the noble philosophy. They care less about style and elegance of words; setting words aside, they want to investigate and state each thing accurately as it really is. Not that they reject the other thing, I think; indeed, they want as much as possible to express their excellent and accurate thoughts in excellent language free from all falsehood. But perhaps they cannot, and it is not so readily available to them: on the one hand, to unfold the sacred and divine faculty in their own words; on the other, to produce speech adorned and polished with words; and to grasp in one and the same small human mind what is the special prerogative of two separate men—especially since the method of each is different and entirely opposed. For silence is in some way friendly to thought and the discovery of things, and a partner in the work; but you would not find the faculty of speaking and dignity of delivery anywhere except in words, and in constant meditation on and use of words. And yet another discipline also violently occupies my mind and completely binds my mouth and tongue, if I should wish to say even a little in the Greek tongue: I mean our wonderful laws, by which the affairs of all who now obey the Roman empire are governed. These are not established or understood without labor and difficulty. They are wise, pious, varied, and admirable—and to sum it up in one word, most Greek. But they are set forth and handed down in the Roman language, which is certainly admirable and magnificent, and suited to the majesty of the empire, but nonetheless heavy and difficult for me. I would never say that I could feel, or be able, or wish otherwise. And since our words are nothing other than certain images of the concepts and notions of our mind, it must be confessed that those who are strong in the faculty of speaking—like certain painters, most skilled in their art and abundantly supplied with colors—can paint not only likenesses but varied ones, made most beautiful by the frequent admixture of flowers, without any hindrance.

But we, like poor men lacking such varied dyes—who either never had them in our art, or perhaps threw them away—paint and fashion the first perceptions of our mind with the words that remain, as if with only charcoal or potsherds, using common names and words. We try to represent the characters of the impressions of the mind in whatever way we can—not clearly, nor adorned for appearance, but as usually happens in charcoal painting. If anything charming and eloquent offers itself, we reject it of our own accord, as people who despise such things. But there is yet a third thing that hinders and calls me away, and much more than the others holds me back and commands me to use silence: the subject itself. I had been eager to speak about it, but now I am forced to hesitate, and I am stuck. For I have set out to speak about a man who seems to be human, and appears so; but to those who can perceive the greatness of his character and habits, he seems endowed with greater and almost divine ornaments.

problems.why: 'viratorum' = 'of greenware/pottery'. 'Potsherds' captures this. 'as if with only' for 'tanquam solis' - correct.

problems.quote: I would never say that I could or would feel otherwise.
problems.source_quote: Non enim aliter sentire aut posse aut velle me unquam dixerim.
problems.why: Drops 'say' (dixerim) and conflates three verbs; meaning is 'I would never say that I feel, can, or will otherwise.'
problems.fix: I would never say that I could feel, or be able, or wish otherwise.
problems.ruling: dixerim 'I would say' is main verb; English misplaces it, conflating 'feel/can/will' as object of 'say' rather than separate verbs governed by dixerim.

problems.why: Glossary term 'testulis' maps to 'potsherds', but 'broken pieces' is banned; however 'potsherds' is used correctly. No issue with 'poor men'.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'no doubt' (nimirum), not 'I mean'; this is an added parenthetical not in the Latin.
last_rejected.ruling: 'I mean' is standard English rendering of explanatory 'nimirum' (lit. 'undoubtedly'); not a misleading addition.

last_rejected.why: 'Commands' is too strong; 'iubet' here means 'bids/urges', not orders.
last_rejected.ruling: 'iubet' normally means 'commands/orders'; 'commands me to use silence' is within normal range. Not a major error.
